info.description:
# Forge API

The NestJS API in `apps/api`, as a collection you can import and send.

## Read this first

**There is no bearer token.** A sign-in returns an opaque session token in a
`Secure`, `HttpOnly` cookie whose name carries the `__Host-` prefix, and the
server keeps the session in Redis (ADR 001). On top of that, **every unsafe
request needs two more things**: a double-submit CSRF token (the `forge_csrf`
cookie, echoed in `X-CSRF-Token`) and an `Origin` the API allows.

Postman is not a browser, so the **collection pre-request script** plays the part
of one. On any request that needs it, the script:

1. has a CSRF token issued — `GET /` sets one for any caller that presents none;
2. signs in with `userEmail` / `userPassword` if no live session token is stored,
   and captures the token from `Set-Cookie` into the environment;
3. attaches `Cookie`, `X-CSRF-Token` and `Origin` to the outgoing request.

So **you never have to run "Sign in" by hand**, and no request needs its own auth
configuration. Requests inherit "No Auth" because the handshake is not one of
Postman's built-in schemes.

The tokens travel as an explicit `Cookie` header rather than through Postman's
cookie jar. That is deliberate: both cookies are `Secure`, and while browsers
special-case `http://localhost` as a trustworthy origin, Postman does not — a
jar-managed session would never be sent to a local API over plain HTTP.

## Setting up

1. Import an environment from `apps/api/postman/environments` and select it.
2. Fill in `userEmail` and `userPassword` **as current values**, so they are not
   written to the file if you export it.
3. Send anything. The first request that needs a session will sign in for you.

No account yet? Run **Account bootstrap** in order: sign up, copy the token out
of the verification link the API prints to its log (`MAIL_PROVIDER=console`), and
verify. `apps/api/postman/README.md` has the long version.

## Conventions

- Errors are `application/problem+json` (RFC 9457) with a stable `type` URI —
  `https://forge.dev/problems/<slug>` — plus `title`, `detail`, `instance` and the
  `requestId` to grep the API log for. Match on the slug, never on the prose.
- Every unsafe route **accepts** `Idempotency-Key` and none requires one. Where
  it is most useful, the header is present but disabled.
- Sensitive lists are throttled per account and per IP with a progressive delay
  rather than a lockout, and answer `429 rate-limited` with `Retry-After`.
- The API is versioned in the path. `baseUrl` includes the prefix and version
  (`/api/v1`), so request paths here start after it.

request.description:
Registers an account and mails a verification link.

`202` with `{ "status": "pending-verification" }` **whether or not the address already has an account** — an address that does gets an "account exists" mail instead, and the response is identical either way so the endpoint is not an account oracle. So a `202` here is not evidence the account is new.

The password must be at least 12 characters, and is additionally checked server-side for strength (`password-too-weak`), breach membership (`password-breached`) and reuse of personal information (`password-uses-personal-information`).

header.description: Only needed when the API runs with TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY set. With it unset — every developer machine — the guard is inert and this header is ignored.

Every unsafe route accepts one; none requires one. Enable this header with a stable value (a UUID) and send twice: the second request replays the first response instead of repeating its effect. Sending a *different* body under the same key is a 409 `idempotency-key-reused`.

request.description:
Exchanges an email and password for a session cookie. The token is in the `Set-Cookie` header and **nowhere else** — never in the body, so a client that logs responses does not log credentials.

Two arms, both of which write a session cookie:

- `{ "user": { … } }` — signed in.
- `{ "status": "mfa_required" }` — the cookie is a half-authenticated session that resolves nothing but the MFA challenge route. Follow with **Complete MFA challenge**.

An unverified address is refused with `email-not-verified`; bad credentials get a deliberately indistinguishable `401 unauthorized`. Repeated failures earn a progressive delay per account and per IP rather than a lockout.

item.description:
Provider sign-in. Both routes are browser redirects rather than JSON, so they are here to be read and copied more than to be sent from Postman.

A provider is configured only when **both** halves of its pair are set (`GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` / `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`, or the Google pair); neither means disabled, and the routes answer `oauth-provider-not-configured`.

**Turn off Postman's *Automatically follow redirects*** (Settings ▸ General) before sending either one, or Postman will chase the `Location` into the provider and you will not see the redirect being tested.

Spends the `state`, exchanges the code, establishes a session and redirects to `APP_URL` with `303 See Other`.

There is deliberately no `returnTo`: a callback that redirected somewhere the caller supplied would be an open redirector attached to a sign-in. The session token is in the `Set-Cookie` and nowhere else — not in the `Location`, not in a fragment.

Sending this by hand needs a `code` and `state` from a real provider round trip, so in practice it is exercised through a browser. The test script captures the session if one was issued.

item.name: Organisations

item.description:
Organisation membership. Roles are `owner`, `admin`, `member` and `billing`.

Each route names the permission it needs, and the service adds the part a decorator cannot express: nobody may promote another member above their own role, and the last owner cannot be demoted or removed.

request.description: Lists the members of the organisation, invited and accepted alike — `acceptedAt` is `null` for an invitation nobody has taken up. Requires `org:members.read`.

originalRequest.description: Lists the members of the organisation, invited and accepted alike — `acceptedAt` is `null` for an invitation nobody has taken up. Requires `org:members.read`.

request.description:
Changes a member's organisation role. Requires `org:members.role-change`.

The guard answers "may this caller change roles here at all"; the service answers "but not to a role above their own, and not away from the last owner". Both refusals are `403 permission-denied`.

Removes a member. Requires `org:members.remove`.

When this returns, the removed member's cached permission set is gone **and** every session they held has been revoked — both after the transaction committed, never before.

item.description:
Inviting somebody to an organisation, and accepting.

Invitations never read the users table (ADR 020), so inviting an address that has no account is ordinary. The token is good for `INVITATION_TTL_SECONDS` — a week, longer than a verification link, because the reader is often not expecting it and may not have an account yet.

request.description:
Accepts an invitation and becomes a member. `201`.

Behind no permission requirement, deliberately: the caller is not a member yet, so their permission set in this organisation is empty and a guard could only ever refuse them. The token is the authorisation.

**Sign in as the invited address first** — accepting binds the invitation to whoever the session belongs to. Point `userEmail` and `userPassword` at that account, or the organisation gains the wrong member.

item.description: Projects inside an organisation. Reads live under `/orgs/{orgId}/projects` so a guest holding a grant and no workspace role can reach them; the listing carries no permission guard at all and simply excludes what the caller cannot read. Writes live under the workspace — `/orgs/{orgId}/workspaces/{workspaceId}/projects` — because the permissions that admit them (`workspace:projects.create`, `workspace:projects.archive`) are workspace-scoped and the guard reads its qualifying id from the path (ADR 031).

request.description:
Creates a project in a workspace; the caller becomes its `owner`. Requires `workspace:projects.create` in that workspace. `201`.

`template` is one of `vite-react`, `nextjs`, `node-api`, `python`, defaults to `vite-react`, and is immutable once chosen. `name` is trimmed, then 1–120 characters.

A viewer, a member with no role in this workspace, a guest and a workspace id from another organisation all get the guard's uniform `403`. The one `404` is an archived workspace the caller still holds a role in.

item.name: Projects

item.description:
Per-project access for one user, above or beside whatever their organisation role gives them. Both routes require `project:share.external`, scoped to the project in the path.

Project roles are `owner`, `editor`, `commenter` and `viewer` — a different vocabulary from organisation roles, and not interchangeable with them.
